 School Board learns why it must refund tax money 
 District on the hook for almost $41,000 refund to Growmark 
 By Fenske Bob 
 on 
 October 22, 2026 
 By Bob Fenske 
 Just as he did last month with the Chickasaw County Board of Supervisors, Chickasaw County Assessor Ray Armel expressed his frustration to the New Hampton School Board on Monday evening about a recent Iowa Supreme Court decision that will cost several governmental taxing entities thousands of dollars during the current fiscal year.   
 Armel wasn’t the only disgruntled person in the room; so, too was School Board President Jay Matthews.   
 In early June, the Supreme Court ruled that the 11 Growmark Inc. 90,000-gallon propane fuel tanks located at the company’s New Hampton fuel terminal should not have been part of the company’s property tax assessments during two fiscal years.   
 Chickasaw County Assessor Ray Armel shares details of an Iowa Supreme Court decision that will force the district to provide a tax refund of almost $41,000 to Growmark Inc.
 The action came after the Chickasaw County Board of Review concluded that the “propane tanks were taxable real property, classifying them as ‘improvements’ under Iowa code.”   
 Growmark appealed that decision to the Property Assessment Appeal Board (PAAB), and that board reversed the decision. The PAAB determined that the propane tanks were unattached equipment and therefore not taxable. 
 In a decision released on June 6, the Supreme Court agreed with Growmark and the PAAB, which means the assessment for Growmark was almost $2 million higher than it should have been.   
 That means entities like the school district, Chickasaw County, Jacksonville Township and others must pay back $81,710.09 to Growmark this fiscal year, and the district was hit the hardest as it is on the hook for $40,997.35 — with the vast majority of that coming from New Hampton’s General Fund.   
 Armel told board members Monday that the decision may have “long-range implications” for assessors and that his frustration came with the Supreme Court reversing what he believes are previous court decisions.   
 Matthews’ frustration came with the fact that the Board of Review’s decision to appeal the PAAB’s ruling came without any feedback from the taxing entities. If the Board of Review hadn’t appealed the case, Matthews pointed out, the district would have been able to collect the taxes from other property owners and not have to refund Growmark.   
 “I guess looking at it from my side … I feel like we’re on the hook for a decision we had no involvement with,” he said. “Because the review board made a decision — and theoretically, if it had turned out different, we wouldn’t be having this conversation — … now, we have to take away $19,000 from our kids because of the decision the Review Board made.”   
 Armel said he understood Matthews’ concerns but added that if the tanks had been removed from the second year of the assessments, that would have doomed the appeal.   
 The assessor did point out that once the Supreme Court made its decision, he was able to remove the tanks from the tax rolls in time for the 2026-27 tax payments. But that came at a price because the district — like the county and the other entities — had already certified its budget with the tanks as part of the tax roll.   
 “So in essence, it’s really a $60,000 hit,” New Hampton Superintendent Erik Smith said, “because we could have gotten the $20,000 this year from other [property owners].”   
 Earlier in the day, the Board of Supervisors agreed to have each entity send checks to the county, which will make one payment to Growmark. County leaders hope to be able to send that refund check to Growmark by the end of the year.
